entries.locator: Schedule, completion promise, and handwritten notes
entries.note: The skipped week, commitment to all ten lectures, notes discussion, and scanner request remain at the opening.

entries.locator: Why the theoretical minimum requires mathematics
entries.note: Exact laws, quantification, direct access to the mathematics, humor, and the age-and-insight exchange are retained.

entries.locator: Upper and lower indices and the scalar differential
entries.note: Coordinate and derivative index families, Einstein summation, metric signs, and the invariant interval are developed in order.
The raised four-gradient and its time-component sign are made explicit.
Stationary action, Euler--Lagrange equations, time translation, and conservation are linked.

entries.locator: Locality, strings, field actions, and entanglement
entries.note: Local propagation, first derivatives, possible nonlocal alternatives, and the distinction between correlation and controllable influence are preserved.

entries.locator: Lorentz invariance, gauge invariance, and dimensions
entries.note: Scalar construction, the curved-spacetime refinement, gauge invariance, and particle-versus-field Lagrangian dimensions remain together.

entries.locator: Necessity of the vector potential and the worldline action
entries.note: The Lorentz-force target, inability to build the required action directly from E and B, and the local A-mu coupling are retained.
The ordinary-time Lagrangian, omitted A-m term, chain rule, and free-versus-dummy-index explanation are carried through.

entries.locator: Grouping electric and magnetic force terms
entries.note: Velocity-independent and antisymmetric velocity-dependent brackets are identified with electric and magnetic forces.
Factors of dt over d tau, four-velocity, proper acceleration, and the field tensor are assembled into a covariant equation.

entries.locator: Four components and local differential dynamics
entries.note: The fourth equation, frame-dependent component lists, remaining coordinate time, and locality as same-time differential dynamics are explained.
Rows, columns, electric and magnetic slots, and the correction concerning mixed-index antisymmetry remain in their recorded sequence.

entries.locator: Constant shifts of a massless scalar
entries.note: The derivative-only massless action is contrasted with the mass term that breaks constant-shift invariance.
Independent coordinates, the changed derivative square, the constant contribution, and the total derivative are preserved.
Adding a four-gradient changes the worldline action only by a fixed-endpoint term.

entries.locator: Direct gauge invariance of the field tensor
entries.note: The transformed tensor is expanded and commuting partial derivatives cancel explicitly.

entries.locator: Redundancy, gauge choice, and Lorentz frames
entries.note: The utility of a nonunique potential and the distinction between local gauge functions and frame transformations are retained.

entries.locator: Gradients and potentials in other field theories
entries.note: The general gradient definition, mathematical-device question, and extension to other potentials remain in order.

entries.locator: Why fundamental interactions are gauge theories
entries.note: The asserted obstruction to a direct E-B action and the broader gauge-theory pattern are reported without inventing a proof.

entries.locator: Observability, nongradient changes, and pure gauge
entries.note: The closing discussion distinguishes measurable field strength, physical nongradient changes, and pure-gauge potentials.

entries.locator: Whether upper and lower labels are arbitrary
entries.note: The names are conventional, but transformation family and contraction structure are not arbitrary.

entries.locator: Why derivatives are lower-index and how to raise them
entries.note: The scalar differential fixes the lower-index transformation, and the metric supplies the raised operator.
Correlations are distinguished from controllable dynamical influence or signaling.
Flat-spacetime scalar construction is contrasted with the scalar-density refinement in gravity.

entries.locator: Dimensions of particle and field Lagrangians
entries.note: A time integral and a spacetime integral require differently dimensioned integrands.

entries.locator: Why introduce A mu when the force uses E and B
entries.note: The potential is required to build the local Lorentz-scalar worldline coupling.
The Cartesian spatial metric leaves spatial component values unchanged.

entries.locator: The missing potential term in canonical momentum
entries.note: The audience catches the omitted minus e A m term and the derivation is corrected before proceeding.

entries.locator: Why a fourth force equation is needed
entries.note: Covariance requires a temporal component paired with the three spatial equations.

entries.locator: Why a fixed numerical list is not intrinsically a vector
entries.note: A two-dimensional rotation example shows that component values depend on the chosen axes.
The intermediate equation was parameterized by coordinate time before conversion to proper time.

entries.locator: Row and column conventions in F mu nu
entries.note: The first index labels the row and the second labels the column.
All-up and all-down tensors are antisymmetric, whereas raising one index changes the visual symmetry of the mixed array.

entries.locator: Whether phi may be shifted by x
entries.note: The proposed nonconstant shift changes the Lagrangian by a constant and a total derivative in the displayed example.

entries.locator: Why partial x over partial t vanishes
entries.note: Coordinate variables are independent in the partial-derivative operation.

entries.locator: Whether Lambda may be any scalar function
entries.note: The gauge parameter is an arbitrary sufficiently regular scalar function.

entries.locator: Practical use of choosing a gauge
entries.note: A convenient representative can simplify equations without changing measurable fields.
Gauge freedom is parameterized by a spacetime function, unlike one global frame transformation.
The gradient is the covector of partial derivatives of a scalar.

entries.locator: Whether gauge freedom is merely a mathematical device
entries.note: The redundancy is mathematical, but it is built into the formulation of fundamental interactions.
Other gauge theories employ analogous potentials with more elaborate internal structure.

entries.locator: Why not write a direct action from E and B
entries.note: The lecture reports the obstruction while explicitly postponing its proof.

entries.locator: Why the fundamental theories are gauge theories
entries.note: Gauge structure is presented as the successful organizing pattern of known interactions.

entries.locator: Whether A mu itself can be measured
entries.note: Only gauge-invariant consequences are directly observable, although the potential is indispensable in the formulation.

entries.locator: What happens under a nongradient change
entries.note: A generic change alters the field tensor; only a pure gradient is gauge redundancy.
Signs are kept consistent with the mostly-plus metric, the stated interaction action, and the field-tensor convention used in Lecture 6.

entries.locator: No-signaling scope of the locality answer
entries.note: The classroom analogy is scoped to uncontrollable correlation versus controllable superluminal influence, not offered as a model of Bell correlations.
The final notes state the correct distinction between antisymmetry of F with both indices in the same position and the mixed array.

entries.locator: Scope of the direct E-B action obstruction
entries.note: The result is identified as an assertion made in the lecture rather than expanded into an unsupported proof.
